title: Augustine (354–430)
hookLine: a brilliant, restless young man hears a child singing take and read and opens the Bible

cards: Milan, the emperor's city. A young professor of rhetoric, paid to make speeches and to teach others to make them. He has a career, admirers, a partner of many years, a son.
And he is miserable. He's been searching for years: philosophy, the Manichees, ambition, pleasure. His mother, Monica, has wept and prayed for him through all of it.
By now he knows he wants to follow Christ. He just can't make himself do it. In the Confessions he owns up to a prayer from his younger years, and it's painfully honest.
In Pusey's translation: "Give me chastity and continency, only not yet."

teach.b: Augustine grew up in North Africa, in what's now Algeria. His book the Confessions tells his life as one long prayer to God, and its turning point is in a garden in Milan.
He's sitting under a fig tree, weeping, sick of himself. From a house nearby he hears a child's voice, singing something like a game, over and over.

teach.h: A CHILD SINGS: TAKE UP AND READ.
teach.b: In Pusey's translation: "Take up and read; Take up and read." He can't think of any children's game with those words.
So he takes it as a sign, goes back to where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on.

teach.h: PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: It's from Romans: not in partying and drunkenness, not in sleeping around, not in fighting and envy, "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says a light flooded his heart and the doubt just went.

He was baptized the next Easter by Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, and Monica saw it before she died. He went home to North Africa and served as a bishop there for the rest of his life, writing constantly.

The Church names him a Doctor of the Church. And the line people carry from him sits on the very first page of the Confessions: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee."
In Augustine's telling, the restlessness isn't only a flaw.

teach.h: OUR HEART IS RESTLESS, UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Augustine on 28 August, the day after his mother Saint Monica, and many read his Confessions as a classic of prayer.

games.q: you're Augustine, weeping under a fig tree. a child's voice nearby keeps singing, take up and read. what do you do?
o: ignore it. it's just a game.
open Paul's letters and read the first thing you see.
games.why: he opens to Romans: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." he says the doubt vanished, and he was baptized that Easter.

practice: If there's a Bible near you, or one on your phone, open it anywhere and read one verse; if there isn't, bring to mind any line of Scripture you already know.
Let it sit without analyzing it, and notice if anything in it catches: not fortune-telling, just letting a word find you. If you pray, you can ask what it's saying to you today.

wordCard.voice: Augustine. The restless, brilliant North African who heard a child sing take up and read, and became a bishop and a Doctor of the Church. Today's word.
